lessons.title: Boolean Values
lessons.introduction: Boolean variables store true or false — the binary foundation of every decision in C++ and Arduino.
objectives: Declare and use bool variables.
Understand how Arduino maps false/0 and true/non-zero.
Store sensor states in readable boolean flags.
conceptExplanation: A bool variable occupies 1 byte and holds either true or false. Naming booleans as yes/no questions — such as isButtonPressed, hasObstacle, or motorRunning — makes your if statements read like plain English.
When printed via Serial.println(), false prints as 0 and true prints as 1.
lessons.analogy: A boolean is a light switch with only two positions: ON (true) or OFF (false) — never 'maybe'.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Boolean Values:
rules: Use descriptive yes/no names like isReady or hasError.
Avoid writing if (isReady == true) — simply write if (isReady).

codeExamples.title: Readable Boolean Flags
codeExamples.description: Stores button press state in a clear boolean variable.

lineByLine.explanation: Converts active-LOW hardware reading into an intuitive true/false flag.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Boolean flags track robot states such as isCalibrated, emergencyStopActive, and targetReached.

commonMistakes.fix: Translate hardware polarity once into a clear bool variable like isPressed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using int when only true/false is needed
commonMistakes.fix: bool communicates intent clearly and prevents invalid states like 2 or -1.

tryItYourself.title: m04_booleans.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Add a second boolean isReleased = !isPressed; and print it.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Serial Monitor prints 1 when pressed and 0 when released.

exercises.prompt: What does Serial.println(true); output in Arduino?
exercises.explanation: Serial.println() prints boolean true as 1 and false as 0.

exercises.prompt: Declare a boolean variable named alarmActive initialized to false.
exercises.explanation: bool is the C++ boolean data type.

summary: bool stores strictly true or false.
Convert active-LOW hardware signals into clear boolean flags.
Serial prints true as 1 and false as 0.

lessons.title: If Statements
lessons.introduction: An if statement runs a block of code only when its condition evaluates to true.
objectives: Write clean single-branch if statements with curly braces.
Trace what happens when the condition is true vs false.
Trigger alerts or outputs based on sensor thresholds.
conceptExplanation: Without decisions, a program runs the exact same instructions forever. An if statement checks a condition inside parentheses ( ); if true, it executes the statements inside { }; if false, it skips the block completely.
lessons.analogy: Think of an if statement like an automatic umbrella: IF it is raining, open the umbrella. Otherwise, keep walking.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for If Statements:
rules: Always wrap the body in { } even for one line to prevent accidental bugs later.
Never put a semicolon right after if (condition).

codeExamples.title: Over-Temperature Warning
codeExamples.description: Prints an alert only when temperature exceeds 40 C.

lineByLine.explanation: Executes because the condition is true.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Thermal cutoffs in 3D printers and motor drivers use if statements to shut down power before components overheat.

commonMistakes.fix: Remove the semicolon so the { } block actually belongs to the if.
Always use { } to keep all intended lines inside the branch.

tryItYourself.title: m04_if.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change motorTempC to 35 and observe that the warning does not print.

exercises.explanation: 3 > 4 is false, so the if block is skipped, and execution continues to Serial.println("Done").

exercises.prompt: Write an if statement that turns LED_PIN HIGH when dist < 15.
exercises.explanation: Checks dist < 15 and writes HIGH inside braces.

summary: if (condition) { ... } runs code only when the condition is true.
Always include curly braces { } and omit trailing semicolons on the if header.
Execution resumes immediately after the closing brace.

lessons.title: If-Else Statements
lessons.introduction: An if-else statement guarantees that exactly one of two mutually exclusive branches runs.
objectives: Write two-way decisions with if and else.
Ensure outputs are explicitly turned OFF in the else branch.
Trace binary hardware control cleanly.
conceptExplanation: When controlling physical hardware like an LED or relay, turning it ON in an if statement is only half the job — you also need to turn it OFF when the condition becomes false! if-else guarantees one branch always executes.
lessons.analogy: A fork in a road: if the bridge is open, go straight; else, take the detour. You always take exactly one path.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for If-Else Statements:
rules: else never takes a condition of its own.
Exactly one of the two blocks executes every time.

codeExamples.title: Button-Controlled LED with if-else
codeExamples.description: Turns LED ON when button is pressed and explicitly OFF when released.

lineByLine.explanation: Guarantees the LED turns back OFF on release.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Door sensors, water-level switches, and limit switches rely on if-else to keep actuators deterministic.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting the else branch on an LED
commonMistakes.fix: Without turning the pin LOW in else, the LED stays stuck ON forever once triggered.
Use else if (condition) when adding another condition; plain else has no parentheses.

tryItYourself.title: m04_if_else.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Add Serial.println("ON") and Serial.println("OFF") inside the two branches with a 200 ms delay.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Pin 8 follows the button cleanly and reports ON/OFF in Serial Monitor.

exercises.prompt: In an if-else statement, how many branches execute on a single pass?
options: It depends on the board voltage
exercises.explanation: Either the if block runs (when true) or the else block runs (when false) — never both.
else defines the block executed when the if condition is false.

summary: if-else handles both true and false outcomes cleanly.
Always turn hardware outputs back OFF in the else branch when appropriate.
Plain else never includes a condition.

lessons.title: Else-If Chains
lessons.introduction: An else-if chain evaluates multiple ordered conditions and runs only the first matching branch.
objectives: Build multi-tier thresholds using if / else if / else.
Order conditions from strictest to broadest so no branch is shadowed.
Design a 3-zone distance warning system.
conceptExplanation: Many robotics decisions have more than two outcomes: for instance, an ultrasonic parking sensor has Danger (<15 cm), Caution (<35 cm), and Safe (>=35 cm). An else-if chain checks each condition in order and stops as soon as one matches.
lessons.analogy: Think of sorting packages by weight: check 'under 1 kg' first, else check 'under 5 kg', else 'heavy freight'.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Else-If Chains:
rules: Order matters! Checking dist < 35 before dist < 15 would swallow the < 15 case.
Include a final else as a safe catch-all.

codeExamples.title: 3-Zone Distance Indicator
codeExamples.description: Categorizes distance into Danger, Caution, and Safe zones.

lineByLine.explanation: Checked second: 22 < 35 is true -> prints CAUTION: SLOW and skips else.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Battery gauges (Full / Medium / Low / Critical) and multi-speed fan controllers use else-if ladders.

commonMistakes.fix: Always order numeric ranges consistently (smallest to largest with <, or largest to smallest with >).

commonMistakes.mistake: Using separate independent ifs when outcomes are mutually exclusive
commonMistakes.fix: Independent ifs can trigger multiple conflicting outputs at once.

tryItYourself.title: m04_else_if.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change distCm to 10 and then to 50 to trace all three zones.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Prints DANGER at 10, CAUTION at 22, and SAFE at 50.

exercises.prompt: What prints if distCm = 12 in this BUGGY order?
exercises.explanation: Because 12 < 35 is true first, the else-if chain exits before ever testing < 15.

exercises.prompt: Add the two-word keyword for a second conditional branch.
exercises.explanation: else if tests an additional condition only when earlier branches were false.

summary: else-if chains select one branch from multiple ordered options.
Always order thresholds carefully so earlier branches don't shadow later ones.
End with a catch-all else for safety.

lessons.title: Nested Conditions
lessons.introduction: A nested condition places one if statement inside another to express multi-stage checks.
objectives: Read and write nested if statements cleanly.
Know when to flatten deep nesting using && for readability.
Apply two-stage guard checks (e.g., system armed -> sensor tripped).
conceptExplanation: Sometimes a second check only makes sense if a first condition is already true — for example, only check the motion sensor if the security system is armed.
Keep nesting shallow (at most 2 levels). If you find yourself 4 levels deep, refactor using && or helper functions.
lessons.analogy: Entering a vault requires unlocking the outer door first; only then can you check the inner safe keypad.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Nested Conditions:
rules: Indent each nested level cleanly so matching braces stay obvious.
Consider combining simple nested ifs with && when there is no outer else.

codeExamples.title: Armed Security Check
codeExamples.description: Checks motion only when the alarm system is armed.

lineByLine.explanation: Outer guard checking whether monitoring is enabled.
Inner decision that runs only while armed.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Autonomous vehicles check whether autonomous mode is enabled (outer) before evaluating lane or obstacle actions (inner).

commonMistakes.fix: Always use { } around both outer and inner blocks and press Ctrl+T in Arduino IDE.

tryItYourself.title: m04_nested.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Set isArmed to false while keeping motion = true and confirm the alert does not fire.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: When isArmed is false, Serial Monitor prints DISARMED regardless of motion.

exercises.prompt: What prints if isArmed = false and motion = true?
exercises.explanation: Because isArmed is false, the inner if is skipped and the outer else prints OFF.

exercises.prompt: When a nested if has no else branches, how can you simplify `if (a) { if (b) { run(); } }`?
exercises.explanation: Combining two simple guards with && flattens nesting and improves readability.

summary: Nested ifs evaluate a second condition inside an outer condition.
Always use explicit { } braces to avoid dangling-else bugs.
Flatten excessive nesting using && or helper functions.

lessons.title: Switch Statements
lessons.introduction: A switch statement cleanly selects one action from many exact integer or character values, ideal for robot modes and Serial commands.
objectives: Write switch-case-break-default blocks.
Explain why omitting break causes fall-through.
Use switch to parse single-letter Serial commands ('F', 'B', 'S').
conceptExplanation: When checking one variable against 4 or more exact values (like mode 0, 1, 2, 3 or Serial commands 'F', 'L', 'R', 'S'), a switch statement is cleaner and easier to read than a long else-if chain.
Every case normally ends with break; so execution exits the switch immediately.
lessons.analogy: A switch statement is like a rotary dial on a washing machine: turn it to a specific mode number and only that cycle runs.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Switch Statements:
rules: switch works on integer and char types (not float or String).
Always include break; at the end of each case unless fall-through is intentional.
Include a default: case to handle unexpected values safely.

codeExamples.title: Serial Robot Command Parser
codeExamples.description: Uses switch to respond to single-character commands.

lineByLine.explanation: Inspects the exact character inside cmd.
Matches 'F', prints Forward, and exits the switch.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Bluetooth-controlled RC robots and menu-driven LCD interfaces use switch statements to dispatch commands cleanly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting break; at the end of a case
commonMistakes.fix: Without break;, execution falls right into the next case and runs it too!

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to switch on a float or String
commonMistakes.fix: Use if/else-if for ranges and Strings; use switch for int, char, or enum.

tryItYourself.title: m04_switch.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Add a case 'L': that prints "Turn Left" and test cmd = 'L'.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: With cmd = 'L', Serial Monitor prints 'Turn Left'.

exercises.prompt: What prints if break; is forgotten after case 1?
exercises.explanation: Without break;, execution falls directly through into case 2.

exercises.prompt: Add the keyword that handles unmatched values in a switch.
exercises.explanation: default: catches any value that does not match an earlier case.

summary: switch cleanly branches on exact int, char, or enum values.
Always end each case with break; unless fall-through is intentional.
Provide a default: case for unexpected inputs.

lessons.title: Compound Conditions
lessons.introduction: Compound conditions combine multiple comparisons with && and || to model realistic multi-sensor robotics logic.
objectives: Write clear compound conditions with explicit parentheses.
Understand short-circuit evaluation in C++.
Guard invalid sensor readings (like timeout -1) before comparing thresholds.
conceptExplanation: In real robotics, sensors sometimes return error codes (like -1 when an ultrasonic pulse times out). A compound condition like if (dist > 0 && dist < 20) first verifies the reading is valid, and only then checks whether an obstacle is close.
C++ uses short-circuit evaluation: in (A && B), if A is false, B is never even evaluated. In (A || B), if A is true, B is skipped.
lessons.analogy: Think of a theme park ride check: (height >= 120 cm) AND (lapBarLocked == true) AND (NOT emergencyStop).

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Compound Conditions:
rules: Always guard invalid values (like dist > 0) on the left side of &&.
Use parentheses whenever mixing && and || in the same expression.

codeExamples.title: Guarded Obstacle Check
codeExamples.description: Ignores timeout (-1.0) while stopping on real close obstacles.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Every reliable ultrasonic or LiDAR obstacle detector uses compound guards so out-of-range timeouts never cause phantom emergency stops.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing only if (distCm < 20.0) when timeout returns -1
commonMistakes.fix: -1 is less than 20, causing false stops! Always require distCm > 0.0 && distCm < 20.0.

tryItYourself.title: m04_compound.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Test distCm = 14.5 and verify STOP prints, then test distCm = -1.0.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Prints DRIVE for -1.0 and STOP for 14.5.

exercises.prompt: Why does `if (dist > 0 && dist < 20)` protect an ultrasonic robot?
options: It stops a timeout value of 0 or -1 from being misread as a close obstacle.
exercises.explanation: Without dist > 0, an error code of 0 or -1 would satisfy dist < 20 and trigger false stops.

exercises.prompt: Write an if condition checking that temp >= 20 AND temp <= 30.

summary: Compound conditions combine multiple checks using &&, ||, and !.
Always guard invalid sensor values on the left side of &&.
Use parentheses to make mixed compound logic unmistakable.
